End-to-End Customer Churn Prediction System¶

Course: Artificial Intelligence – Final Project (Batch 3) · Question 1 Models: Logistic Regression and K-Nearest Neighbours · Dataset: IBM Telco Customer Churn (7,043 customers, 21 columns)

1. Problem statement¶

A telecom company loses revenue every time a customer leaves (churns). Keeping an existing customer is usually much cheaper than acquiring a new one, so the goal is to predict which customers are likely to churn from their historical account data, so the retention team can contact them first.

This is a binary classification problem: Churn = Yes (1) or No (0).

Pipeline: Load → EDA → Clean missing values → Encode categoricals → Split → Scale → Train (LR, KNN) → Evaluate → Overfitting vs underfitting → Conclusions.

import os, warnings

# Only 11 rows (0.16%). Median imputation keeps every row and is robust to the right-skew of TotalCharges.
median_tc = df['TotalCharges'].median()
df['TotalCharges'] = df['TotalCharges'].fillna(median_tc)
print('Median used:', median_tc, '| missing now:', df.isna().sum().sum())
df = df.drop(columns='customerID')   # identifier, carries no signal
print('Rows identical in every feature:', df.duplicated().sum(), '(kept: after removing the ID they are different customers with similar plans)')

Median used: 1397.475 | missing now: 0
Rows identical in every feature: 22 (kept: after removing the ID they are different customers with similar plans)

Decision: median imputation (not mean, because TotalCharges is right-skewed; not drop, to avoid losing rows). customerID is an identifier so it is removed.

5. Encode categorical variables¶

In [10]:
# Binary Yes/No columns -> label encoding (0/1); multi-category columns -> one-hot encoding
df['Churn'] = (df['Churn']=='Yes').astype(int)
df['gender'] = (df['gender']=='Male').astype(int)
yes_no = ['Partner','Dependents','PhoneService','PaperlessBilling']
for c in yes_no: df[c] = (df[c]=='Yes').astype(int)

multi = [c for c in df.select_dtypes('object').columns]
print('One-hot encoding:', multi)
df_enc = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=multi, drop_first=True, dtype=int)
print('Shape after encoding:', df_enc.shape)

drop_first=True removes one dummy per feature to avoid the dummy-variable trap (perfect multicollinearity), which matters for Logistic Regression.

6. Train/test split and feature scaling¶

In [12]:
X = df_enc.drop(columns='Churn'); y = df_enc['Churn']
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
print('Train:', X_train.shape, '| Test:', X_test.shape)
print('Churn rate train/test:', round(y_train.mean(),3), round(y_test.mean(),3))

num_cols = ['tenure','MonthlyCharges','TotalCharges']
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train[num_cols])          # fit on TRAIN only -> no data leakage
X_train_s, X_test_s = X_train.copy(), X_test.copy()
X_train_s[num_cols] = scaler.transform(X_train[num_cols])
X_test_s[num_cols]  = scaler.transform(X_test[num_cols])
X_train_s[num_cols].describe().loc[['mean','std']].round(3)

Train: (5634, 30) | Test: (1409, 30)
Churn rate train/test: 0.265 0.265
Out[12]:
tenure MonthlyCharges TotalCharges
mean -0.0 -0.0 -0.0
std 1.0 1.0 1.0

The split is stratified so both sets keep the same churn rate. The scaler is fitted on the training set only and then applied to the test set, so no test information leaks into training. Scaling matters most for KNN (distance-based): without it, TotalCharges (0–8,000) would drown out binary features.

7. Train the models¶

In [13]:
# Choose K for KNN with 5-fold CV on the training set (never touching the test set)
cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
ks = list(range(1, 52, 2))
cv_scores = [cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(k), X_train_s, y_train, cv=cv, scoring='f1').mean() for k in ks]
best_k = ks[int(np.argmax(cv_scores))]
print('Best K by CV F1:', best_k, '| CV F1 =', round(max(cv_scores),4))

lr  = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_train_s, y_train)
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=best_k).fit(X_train_s, y_train)

Best K by CV F1: 35 | CV F1 = 0.6088

8. Evaluate and compare the models¶

In [14]:
def evaluate(name, model):
    p = model.predict(X_test_s)
    return {'Model':name, 'Accuracy':accuracy_score(y_test,p), 'Precision':precision_score(y_test,p),
            'Recall':recall_score(y_test,p), 'F1-score':f1_score(y_test,p),
            'ROC-AUC':roc_auc_score(y_test, model.predict_proba(X_test_s)[:,1])}

results = pd.DataFrame([evaluate('Logistic Regression', lr), evaluate(f'KNN (k={best_k})', knn)]).set_index('Model').round(4)
results.to_csv('evaluation_summary.csv')
results

How to read these metrics (churn = positive class)¶

  • Accuracy – share of all predictions that are correct. Misleading on imbalanced data.
  • Precision – of customers we flagged as churners, how many really churned (cost of wasted retention offers).
  • Recall – of customers who really churned, how many we caught (cost of lost customers). This is usually the metric the business cares about most.
  • F1-score – harmonic mean of precision and recall; one balanced number.
  • Confusion matrix – the raw counts: TN, FP, FN, TP.

9. Overfitting vs. underfitting¶

  • Underfitting (high bias): the model is too simple, so it does badly on both training and test data.
  • Overfitting (high variance): the model memorises the training data, so it scores very high on training data but noticeably worse on unseen data.
  • Good fit: training and test scores are both reasonable and close together.

KNN lets us see this directly: K is the complexity knob. K=1 gives a jagged boundary that memorises every point (overfit); a very large K averages over too many neighbours and the boundary becomes too smooth (underfit).

In [17]:
ks2 = [1,3,5,9,15,25,35,50,75,100,150,250,400,700,1200,2000]
tr, te = [], []
for k in ks2:
    m = KNeighborsClassifier(k).fit(X_train_s, y_train)
    tr.append(f1_score(y_train, m.predict(X_train_s))); te.append(f1_score(y_test, m.predict(X_test_s)))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4.5))
ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.plot(ks2, tr, 'o-', label='Train F1', color='#4C78A8'); ax.plot(ks2, te, 's-', label='Test F1', color='#E45756')
ax.axvline(best_k, ls='--', color='gray', label=f'Chosen k={best_k}')
ax.annotate('Overfitting\n(big train-test gap)', xy=(ks2[0], tr[0]), xytext=(1.6, .85), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='black'))
ax.annotate('Underfitting\n(both scores collapse)', xy=(ks2[-1], te[-1]), xytext=(150, .72), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='black'))
ax.set_xlabel('K (log scale) - simpler model to the right'); ax.set_ylabel('F1-score'); ax.set_title('KNN: complexity vs. performance'); ax.legend()
save('07_overfitting_underfitting'); plt.show()
In [18]:

10. Bonus: what drives churn? (Logistic Regression coefficients)¶

In [19]:
coef = pd.Series(lr.coef_[0], index=X.columns).sort_values()
top = pd.concat([coef.head(8), coef.tail(8)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,6))
ax.barh(top.index, top.values, color=['#4C78A8' if v<0 else '#E45756' for v in top.values])
ax.set_title('Top Logistic Regression coefficients\n(red = raises churn risk, blue = lowers it)'); ax.axvline(0,color='k',lw=.8)
save('08_lr_coefficients'); plt.show()

Reading the coefficients: positive = higher churn risk, negative = lower, holding other features fixed. Fibre-optic internet is the biggest risk factor; two-year contracts and long tenure are the biggest protectors. Caution: MonthlyCharges shows a negative sign even though churners pay more in raw data, because it is strongly correlated with the internet/streaming dummies (multicollinearity), which absorb its effect. Interpret individual coefficients of correlated features carefully.

11. Bonus: improving recall on the imbalanced data¶

In [20]:
lr_bal = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight='balanced', random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_train_s, y_train)
p = lr_bal.predict(X_test_s)
final = pd.concat([results, pd.DataFrame([{'Accuracy':accuracy_score(y_test,p),'Precision':precision_score(y_test,p),'Recall':recall_score(y_test,p),
   'F1-score':f1_score(y_test,p),'ROC-AUC':roc_auc_score(y_test, lr_bal.predict_proba(X_test_s)[:,1])}], index=['Logistic Regression (balanced)']).round(4)])
final.index.name='Model'; final.to_csv('evaluation_summary.csv'); final
Out[20]:
Accuracy Precision Recall F1-score ROC-AUC
Model
Logistic Regression 0.8055 0.6572 0.5588 0.6040 0.8421
KNN (k=35) 0.7942 0.6173 0.5909 0.6038 0.8338
Logistic Regression (balanced) 0.7388 0.5052 0.7834 0.6143 0.8417

class_weight='balanced' penalises missing a churner more heavily. Recall rises sharply at the cost of some precision and accuracy: a worthwhile trade when a lost customer costs more than an unnecessary retention call.

12. Conclusions¶

In [21]:
best = results['F1-score'].idxmax()
print(f'Best baseline model by F1: {best}')
print(final.to_string())

Best baseline model by F1: Logistic Regression
                                Accuracy  Precision  Recall  F1-score  ROC-AUC
Model                                                                         
Logistic Regression               0.8055     0.6572  0.5588    0.6040   0.8421
KNN (k=35)                        0.7942     0.6173  0.5909    0.6038   0.8338
Logistic Regression (balanced)    0.7388     0.5052  0.7834    0.6143   0.8417

Findings

  1. Churn is driven by short tenure, month-to-month contracts, fibre-optic service and electronic-check payment; long-term contracts and tenure strongly protect against churn.
  2. The two models are very close on F1 (0.604 vs 0.604). Logistic Regression is slightly better on accuracy, precision and ROC-AUC; KNN catches a few more churners (higher recall) but raises more false alarms.
  3. Logistic Regression is the recommended model: equal F1, no train/test gap (it generalises), instant to train and predict, and its coefficients are directly explainable to the business. KNN is sensitive to K (see the overfitting plot), shows a small train-test gap, and is slower at prediction time.
  4. Accuracy (~80%) looks good but hides that the baseline models still miss about 4 in 10 churners (recall ≈ 56-59%). The balanced logistic regression raises recall to about 78%, at the cost of accuracy and precision.

Business recommendations: offer incentives to move month-to-month customers onto 1–2-year contracts, focus onboarding and support on the first 6 months, and review the fibre-optic pricing/quality and the electronic-check experience.

Limitations / next steps: one dataset and one train/test split; try tree-based models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting), threshold tuning, and cost-sensitive evaluation.
